newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia warns groups against East Timor meeting.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia warns groups against East Timor meeting.

text.p: The Malaysian government on Wednesday said it has advised human rights groups against going ahead with a planned conference on East Timor, but stopped short of saying it was banned.
"I have advised them (against holding the meeting)," Deputy Home Minister Megat Junid Megat Ayob told foreign journalists.
He said the government would have to act if the meeting generated anti-Indonesia protests.
"If there are protests, we cannot keep quiet," he said after holding a closed-door meeting about the conference with editors of local news organisations.

Asked what the government planned to do if the groups went ahead with the three-day meeting beginning on Saturday, Megat Junid said: "We'll see what happens. We'll cross that border when we come to it."
A conference spokeswoman said on Wednesday the meeting was legal and would go ahead despite the Malaysian government's objections.
"We're not about to go running into the streets," said Debbie Stothard. "We will be engaging in peaceful and legitimate activities."
About 200 people from 24 countries and 75 organisations are expected to attend the conference in Kuala Lumpur, she said.

The deputy home minister asked editors at Wednesday's meeting to avoid further coverage of the conference, local journalists said. But they said the government would not stop the meeting or prevent foreign journalists from covering it.
Megat Junid said on Monday the government opposed the conference for fear of harming its ties with Indonesia.

Conference organisers said Jose Ramos-Horta, the East Timorese activist who last month was named co-winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, would not attend the meeting if it would cause problems between Malaysia and Indonesia. They added it was uncertain whether the other winner, East Timor's Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo, would attend.
Indonesia invaded east Timor in December 1975 and annexed the former Portuguese colony the following year. The United Nations still recognises Lisbon as the administering authority for the territory.
